subject: political-science
lectureTitle: EU I: The Evolution of the EU (AUW)
part: Part III · The European Union as a Political System
readings: McCormick, *Understanding the EU* (2021) pp. 45–66 · Wiener, Börzel & Risse, *European Integration Theory* (2019): neofunctionalism pp. 44–49, liberal intergovernmentalism pp. 64–70

cards.front: Define **European integration** as a *process* — and name the three things that shift to the "new centre" in **Haas's (1958)** classic definition.
cards.back:
Integration = a **process** by which states **increasingly cooperate, create common rules & institutions, and exercise some authority *jointly*** — changing *where* decisions are made and *what* states can do alone vs together.

**Haas (1958):** political actors are persuaded to shift their **loyalties, expectations and political activities** toward a new centre whose institutions demand jurisdiction over the pre-existing states.

It is at once **institutional** (building shared bodies) and **political** (contested, driven by interests).
cards.hint: Loyalties · expectations · activities.

cards.front: A definition says integration means actors shifting their **"loyalties, expectations and political activities toward a new centre."** Whose definition is this — and why is the definition *itself* significant for the theory section?
cards.back:
**Ernst Haas (1958)**, in *The Uniting of Europe*.

The significance: the definition is **already neofunctionalist** — it builds in the transformative claim that integration *changes actors' loyalties*, pulling them upward. Choosing this definition quietly loads the dice toward one of the two rival theories.
cards.hint: The founder of neofunctionalism.

cards.front: The EU is called ***sui generis*** — "neither a typical international organization nor a state." Explain both halves of the claim.
cards.back:
**Unlike an ordinary IO:** its institutions **exercise real, binding authority** where states have **transferred or pooled** powers — sometimes by **majority**, so a state can be **outvoted**. Ordinary IOs can't bind members this way.

**Unlike a state:** there is **no single European sovereign government** replacing the member states, who **remain sovereign**.

The EU is a **new kind of political animal** — a *mix* of supranational and intergovernmental governance, which is exactly why the two theories fight over how to read it.
cards.hint: Real authority (unlike an IO) but no single sovereign (unlike a state).

cards.front: Distinguish **supranational** from **intergovernmental** governance — the master distinction of the whole Part.
cards.back:
**Supranational** = authority **above** the states: common institutions (**Commission, Court, Parliament, ECB**) make and enforce rules that bind members, sometimes by **majority** (a state can be outvoted). Like a would-be federation.

**Intergovernmental** = authority **between** the states: decisions taken by governments bargaining as **sovereign equals**, each keeping a **veto**. Like a club of states.

The EU **combines both** — supranational in some policy areas, intergovernmental in others.
cards.hint: Above the states vs between the states.

cards.front: Integration grows in **two directions at once**. Name and contrast them — with the "vertical/horizontal" labels and an example of each.
cards.back:
**DEEPENING** — the **scope & depth** of integration grows: more policy areas become European, common institutions gain more authority. **"Vertical"** — authority moves *upward*. E.g. ECSC → single market → euro.

**WIDENING** — the **territory** grows: more **states join**. **"Horizontal"** — the club gets *bigger*. E.g. 6 → 9 → 12 → 15 → 25 → 27 → 28.

They often happen **together** (SEA deepening alongside Southern enlargement) but can **pull against** each other — a wider, more diverse EU is harder to deepen (more vetoes), which is why **Nice (2001)** had to reform the institutions.
cards.hint: Vertical (deeper) vs horizontal (wider).

cards.front: The take-home exercise: classify each event as **deepening, widening, both, or reversal** — (a) Maastricht & the euro; (b) the 2004 "big-bang"; (c) the Single European Act + Southern enlargement; (d) Brexit.
cards.back:
(a) **Deepening** — same members, much more shared authority (a pure *vertical* jump).
(b) **Widening** — 10 new members, no new depth that year (a pure *horizontal* stretch).
(c) **Both** — the single-market push (deepen) coincided with Greece/Spain/Portugal joining (widen).
(d) **Reversal / disintegration** — a member *leaves*; the path moves **left** for the first time.

Full set of possibilities: **deepening · widening · both · contestation · disintegration.**
cards.hint: Vertical jump · horizontal stretch · diagonal · leftward.

cards.front: The EU was "**born out of the ruins of WWII**." Run **McCormick's three post-war needs** that drove integration — and name the master key that unlocked them.
cards.back:
**Three needs:** ① rebuild shattered **economies** (agricultural output had *halved*) → ② provide **security** as the USSR loomed and the Cold War set in → ③ **tame nationalism** (the nation-state "discredited by the war").

**The master key = Franco-German reconciliation.** Bind the two historic enemies together and broader integration could follow — so the first step was **coal & steel**, the base of German (Ruhr) power: pooling them made West Germany reliant on its neighbours *and* eased French fear of German revival.
cards.hint: Economy → security → nationalism; unlocked by binding France & Germany.

cards.front: Integration was "**underwritten by the US**." Name the **two pieces of American scaffolding** and what each contributed.
cards.back:
**① Marshall Plan (1948–51)** — ~**$12.5 bn** of US aid channelled via the **OEEC (Paris)**; it *encouraged European governments to work together* and exposed their economic **interdependence**.

**② NATO (1949)** — the **security shield** ("an attack on one = an attack on all") under which integration could safely proceed.
cards.hint: One economic, one military — both American.

cards.front: The founders' **false start**: an ambitious **European Defence Community** was proposed in 1950 but collapsed. What killed it — and what *lesson* did the founders draw?
cards.back:
The **French National Assembly rejected the EDC in 1954** — no British support, French fear of German rearmament, national humiliation at **Dien Bien Phu**.

**Lesson:** integrate through **low-politics economics first** (Monnet's *"step by step through concrete achievements"*), *not* high-politics defence.

This is exactly the sequence **neofunctionalism** later theorised — and **Suez (1956)** hammered it home: Britain & France found they were no longer world powers.
cards.hint: Defence-first failed; economics-first became the strategy.

cards.front: Trace the founding sequence **from coal & steel to a common market (1950–68)** — the four steps neofunctionalists read as spillover.
cards.back:
**① Schuman Declaration (9 May 1950)** — drafted by **Monnet**, announced by **Schuman**: pool Franco-German coal & steel under a common **High Authority**, a "first step in the federation of Europe," making war "**materially impossible**."
→ **② ECSC (Treaty of Paris 1951, began 1952)** — the **Six** build the **first supranational** body; modest, but "proved the feasibility of integration."
→ **③ Treaties of Rome (1957) → EEC + Euratom** — commit to a **common market** in 12 years (free movement of people, money, services + common external tariff).
→ **④ Customs union (1968)**, formed *ahead* of schedule, + the **CAP**.

This early momentum looked like a **vindication of neofunctionalism.**
cards.hint: Schuman → ECSC → Rome/EEC → customs union + CAP.

cards.front: Name the crisis: in **1965–66 de Gaulle boycotted the Council** over Commission power, voting and the budget — and name the compromise that ended it and what it restored.
cards.back:
The **empty-chair crisis (1965–66)**, ended by the **Luxembourg Compromise (1966)**, which **affirmed the national veto.**

Significance: it directly **contradicted neofunctionalism's assumption of automaticity** — the state "struck back" — and became the **first big evidence for the intergovernmental side.** Haas later called his theory **"obsolescent" (1976).**
cards.hint: De Gaulle's empty chair; the veto returns.

cards.front: Give the **evolution timeline on one page** — the milestone for each: 1951/52 · 1957/58 · 1973 · 1986/87 · 1992/93 · 1999/2002 · 2009 · 2016/2020.
cards.back:
**1951/52 — ECSC** (Treaty of Paris; first supranational transfer) · *deepen*
**1957/58 — Treaties of Rome → EEC + Euratom** (common market goal) · *deepen*
**1973 — first enlargement** (UK, Ireland, Denmark) · *widen*
**1986/87 — Single European Act** (single market by 1992) · *deepen*
**1992/93 — Maastricht → "the European Union"** (pillars, EMU, citizenship) · *deepen*
**1999/2002 — the euro** (electronic then notes & coins) · *deepen*
**2009 — Treaty of Lisbon** (salvaged from the rejected Constitution) · *deepen*
**2016/2020 — Brexit** (referendum → UK leaves) · *reverse*
cards.hint: ECSC → Rome → enlargements → SEA → Maastricht/euro → Lisbon → Brexit.

cards.front: Trace the **enlargements from 6 to 28** in waves — and note what each wave changed.
cards.back:
**1973 — UK, Ireland, Denmark** (UK had been **vetoed twice by de Gaulle**, who feared US influence; **Norway** said no).
**1981/86 — Southern:** Greece, then Spain & Portugal — anchoring **new democracies** after dictatorship; doubling to 12 **reduced Franco-German dominance.**
**1995 — Austria, Finland, Sweden** (rich EFTA states).
**2004 "big-bang" — 10 states** (8 post-communist + Cyprus, Malta); **2007** Bulgaria & Romania; **2013** Croatia → **28 members, ~500 m people** — symbolically the **end of the Cold War division.**

cards.front: Name the 1993 conditions applicants (mainly Eastern) had to meet to join — list all three — and the term for the whole body of existing EU law one of them requires adopting.
cards.back:
The **Copenhagen criteria (1993):** (a) stable **democracy**, human rights, rule of law; (b) a functioning **market economy**; (c) capacity to adopt the **acquis communautaire** — the whole existing body of EU law.

Significance: enlargement wasn't just adding territory — it **drove domestic change** in applicants. This is **"conditionality."**
cards.hint: Democracy · market economy · adopt the *acquis*.

cards.front: From the mid-1980s integration went **political, not just economic**. Trace the deepening arc: **SEA → Maastricht → euro → Lisbon.**
cards.back:
**Single European Act (1986/87)** — complete the **single market by 31 Dec 1992** (scrap controls, harmonise standards, mutual recognition); made **EMU an objective.**
**Maastricht (1992/93) → "the European Union"** — the **three-pillar** structure, **EMU (Delors plan)** confirmed, **EU citizenship**, EP **codecision.**
**The euro** — electronic **1999**, notes & coins **2002** (opt-outs: Denmark, Sweden, UK); members surrender **national monetary policy** — a clear example of **deepening.**
**Lisbon (2009)** — salvaged from the Constitution killed by French & Dutch referendums (2005): permanent **European Council President**, a **High Representative**, **pillars abolished**, more **QMV**, and **Article 50** (right to leave).
cards.hint: Single market → Union → single currency → Lisbon.

cards.front: Name the treaty and its **three-pillar** structure: (1) ___, (2) ___, (3) ___ — and say which pillars were intergovernmental and what later abolished them.
cards.back:
The **Maastricht Treaty (1992/93)**:
**(1) the European Community** · **(2) Common Foreign & Security Policy (CFSP)** · **(3) Justice & Home Affairs (JHA)**.

**Pillars 2 & 3 were intergovernmental**; they were **abolished by the Treaty of Lisbon (2009)**, giving the EU a single legal personality.
cards.hint: EC · CFSP · JHA; killed by Lisbon.

cards.front: Define the shift from **"permissive consensus" to politicization** — a key exam concept — and name the event that broke the old consensus.
cards.back:
**Permissive consensus** = the old, quietly **elite-driven** phase: publics barely noticed and let elites decide (recall neofunctionalism's assumption).

It **broke down after the Danish "no" to Maastricht (1992)**. Integration became **politicized** — tied to hot issues: **economic distribution, national sovereignty, migration & borders, identity.** Enter **Euroscepticism.**
cards.hint: Elites quietly deciding → loud public contestation, from 1992.

cards.front: From the late 2000s the EU hit a **"polycrisis"** (Juncker) — McCormick's **Seven Crises**. Name them roughly in order.
cards.back:
① **Constitutional Treaty** failure (2005) → ② **global financial crisis** (from 2007, imported from the US crash) → ③ **euro / sovereign-debt crisis** (from 2009 — Greece's ~**13%** deficit vs the 3% limit; bailouts by EU/**ECB**/**IMF** conditional on **austerity**; "Grexit" fears) → ④ **rule-of-law crisis** (**Hungary & Poland**; Orbán) → ⑤ **refugee crisis** (Syrian war; 2014–15; the EU–**Turkey** deal) → ⑥ **Brexit** → ⑦ **Covid-19** (2020 — the only crisis with no EU-internal cause).

Each became a **moment when the scope, limits & distribution of cooperation were contested** — great material for both theories.
cards.hint: Constitution · finance · euro · rule-of-law · refugees · Brexit · Covid.

cards.front: **Brexit** — in June 2016 UK voters chose to leave (**52%–48%**, 72% turnout); the UK left in Jan 2020. What theoretical point does it make, and what were McCormick's two readings of it?
cards.back:
**The point:** integration is **not one-directional** — the arrow can point **left**. The full set is deepening · widening · contestation · **and disintegration.**

**What it revealed:** Leave support was highest among **older, less-educated** voters, rode **low public knowledge** and a broader **rejection of globalization.**

**Two readings:** either a **warning** of the costs of leaving (a chance for the 27 to *deepen*, e.g. defence) — *or*, more darkly (Bellamy & Castiglione), a sign of **"fragmentation and political disintegration."**
cards.hint: The arrow can point left; warning vs disintegration.

cards.front: A theory says integration is **semi-automatic and expansive** — one step forces the next, carried by **elites and supranational bureaucrats**, changing actors' very **loyalties**. Name the theory, its founder, and its master concept.
cards.back:
**Neofunctionalism** — founder **Ernst Haas**, *The Uniting of Europe* (1958), written to explain the **ECSC**; revised by **Lindberg** & **Schmitter**; rooted in **Mitrany's functionalism.**

**Master concept: spillover.** Integration is **incremental, elite-driven, positive-sum and self-expanding** — actors "**stumble**" from one decision to the next, often under "the pressure of crises and impending deadlines." Institutions, once created, **acquire autonomy** and push for more.
cards.hint: Spillover; Haas; loyalties shift upward.

cards.front: A theory says integration is a **"series of rational choices made by national leaders"** — states are the **"masters of the treaty"** and the EU is "an international regime for policy coordination." Name the theory, its founder, and its two core assumptions.
cards.back:
**Liberal Intergovernmentalism (LI)** — founder **Andrew Moravcsik**, *The Choice for Europe* (1998); roots in **Hoffmann's** intergovernmentalism (1966). Today the field's **"baseline" theory.**

**Two assumptions:** ① states are the **critical, unitary actors** (bargaining as sovereign equals); ② they are **boundedly rational** (calculate costs/benefits, maximise utility).

But LI is **not realism** — it takes **domestic economic interests** seriously and treats institutions as useful. It unfolds as a clean **three-stage model.**
cards.hint: Moravcsik; "masters of the treaty"; unitary + boundedly rational.

cards.front: Run **spillover** — neofunctionalism's master mechanism — in its **three types**. Who/what drives each, and how does each create pressure?
cards.back:
Spillover = integration in one area **creates pressure to integrate others** (Haas's "expansive logic of sector integration").

**① Functional** — driven by the **technical interdependence** of sectors: integrating one creates **practical problems** solvable only by integrating the **adjacent** one (expands almost mechanically).
**② Political** — driven by **national elites & interest groups**: they **shift expectations, lobbying and loyalties** to the European level; repeated contact breeds **"bureaucratic interpenetration"** and socialization.
**③ Cultivated** — driven by **supranational institutions** (Commission / High Authority): the "Eurocrats" **broker** deals, "splitting the difference" and **"upgrading common interests."**
cards.hint: Technical problems · shifting loyalties · Eurocrats brokering.

cards.front: Name the type of spillover: (a) free movement of workers forces integrated **social-security, tax, pension & qualification** rules; (b) firms & unions **move their lobbying** to Brussels; (c) the **Commission** brokers a package deal that "upgrades common interests."
cards.back:
(a) **Functional spillover** — one integrated sector creates practical problems in adjacent ones.
(b) **Political spillover** — elites/interest groups shift expectations & loyalties upward.
(c) **Cultivated spillover** — supranational institutions actively broker further integration.

(The deck's worked example: an Austrian professional living, working and retiring in **Portugal** needs all of those rules integrated — functional spillover in action.)
cards.hint: Adjacent-sector problems · lobbying moves up · Commission brokers.

cards.front: Run **Moravcsik's three-stage model** of how any integration decision is made — the stage, its question, and the theory that explains each.
cards.back:
**① National preferences** — *what does each state want?* → a **liberal** theory: preferences are **issue-specific**, built **bottom-up** from **domestic economic & societal interests** (producers vs taxpayers), not a single goal like "security."
**② Interstate bargaining** — *what deal, and who gains?* → an **intergovernmental** theory: **hard bargaining** over the distribution of gains; power flows from **asymmetrical interdependence.**
**③ Institutional choice** — *why build institutions?* → a **regime** theory: institutions **lock in credible commitments** and cut transaction costs.
cards.hint: Preferences → bargaining → institutions (liberal → intergovernmental → regime).

cards.front: In LI, name the source of bargaining power captured by the rule *"the state that needs the deal least is the most powerful."* And name the two ways states handle sovereignty when building institutions.
cards.back:
**Asymmetrical interdependence** — the less-dependent state can most credibly **walk away** (its **"outside option"** is better), so big states dominate and outcomes tend toward the **lowest common denominator.**

**Two ways to handle sovereignty:**
• **Pooling** — deciding together, e.g. **qualified-majority voting.**
• **Delegating** — handing authority to a body (**Commission, ECB, ECJ**).

States do this not to lose control but to make **commitments credible** — a **prisoner's-dilemma** fix against later defection.
cards.hint: Better outside option = more power; pool vs delegate.

cards.front: Put **neofunctionalism** and **liberal intergovernmentalism** side by side: who's in charge, what drives integration, how they treat supranational institutions, and what each explains best/worst.
cards.back:
**Who's in charge:** NF — elites, interest groups, firms & **supranational institutions**; LI — **states** ("masters of the treaty").
**What drives it:** NF — **spillover** (semi-automatic, positive-sum, "upgrading common interests"); LI — **rational state choices** (preferences → distributive **hard bargaining** → institutions).
**Supranational institutions:** NF — **autonomous engines** that reshape national interests; LI — **endogenous instruments** to make commitments credible.
**Loyalties shift upward?** NF **yes**; LI **no.**
**Explains well:** NF — the **expansive early phase** (ECSC→EEC) & everyday "creep"; LI — the **grand treaty bargains** (Rome, SEA, Maastricht).
**Explains badly:** NF — the **empty-chair crisis / de Gaulle**; LI — **everyday politics** & autonomous supranational agency.
cards.hint: Runaway logic vs controlled bargains.

cards.front: **The eurozone / sovereign-debt crisis, explained twice.** Show how neofunctionalism and LI read the *same* deepening (tighter EMU) differently — driver, mechanism, key actors, outcome.
cards.back:
**Neofunctionalist reading:** a **functional gap** in EMU's design created **spillover** — monetary policy was pooled at the supranational level while **fiscal** policy stayed national, generating pressure to close the gap. Actors: **BusinessEurope**, markets, Commission, Parliament, even the **ECB** (which "breached impartiality" to demand a **Banking Union**). Outcome: crisis + deadlines → **incremental deepening**, institutions seeking autonomy.

**LI reading:** **member states bargained over who pays.** Mechanism: **hard bargaining** over bailouts, rescue funds, the Fiscal Compact. Actors: a **Northern vs Southern** coalition, the North holding more **bargaining power.** Outcome: the North **delayed support** to force the South to accept the **Fiscal Compact** (budget monitoring / European Semester).

**The point:** the *same* deepening = **spillover** (NF) *or* a **distributional bargain** (LI). Neither is obviously wrong — that's why we keep two theories.
cards.hint: Functional gap forcing the next step vs creditors extracting austerity.

cards.front: The essay takeaway: don't treat the two theories as right/wrong but as **two lenses.** State where each is strongest — and name the reusable four-step exam template.
cards.back:
**Two lenses:** **Neofunctionalism** is strongest where integration seems to **outrun** what governments planned (spillover, unintended consequences, Commission creep). **LI** is strongest at the **big set-piece treaty moments** where governments visibly **bargain hard** over terms.

A good answer names **which phenomenon** each explains best — and uses the **eurozone case** to show the *same* event through both.

**The four-step template:** **claim → mechanism → evidence → how the *other* theory would explain the same facts.** (Take-home: run it on **EU defence integration.**)
cards.hint: Outrunning states vs bargaining hard; claim → mechanism → evidence → rival.
